query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of chromium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby enhancing oxygen resistance relative to the alloy without added Cr.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy composed of refractory elements (e.g., W, Mo, Ta, Nb, etc.) without chromium doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled addition of chromium (e.g., ~5–10 atomic percent) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloy to an oxidizing environment (static air with ~21% O2) at approximately 1000 °C for a duration of 50 hours, possibly including thermal cycling to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added chromium oxidizes preferentially to form a protective Cr2O3 layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, limiting further oxidation of the underlying alloy. This inhibited oxygen transport decreases the overall oxidation rate compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cr-doped alloy will exhibit lower oxide weight gain, improved scale adhesion, and a more uniform oxide film than the untreated alloy under the same high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys without chromium show higher oxygen uptake and more spallation-prone, discontinuous oxide scales under similar high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected within a temperature window around 1000 °C in standard air; at higher temperatures (e.g., >1200 °C) or in extremely aggressive oxidizing environments, the protective effect may diminish or other deleterious phases might form.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal chromium concentration that maximizes oxidation resistance without compromising other mechanical properties (e.g., due to brittle intermetallic formation) is not precisely known and requires additional optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the refractory high-entropy alloy doped with ~5–10 at.% Cr and a control set with identical base composition but without Cr. Subject both sets to oxidation at 1000 °C in static air for 50 hours (with optional thermal cycling to simulate service conditions). After exposure, measure the mass gain per unit area and analyze the surface oxide layer’s uniformity, phase composition (via X-ray diffraction), and adhesion (via microscopy and scratch tests).
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity (via SEM or optical microscopy)
Phase identification of the oxide scale (using XRD)
Adhesion quality of the oxide scale (via scratch tests or adhesion measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide mass gain and enhanced scale continuity/adhesion compared to the control alloy under the defined conditions, or if the addition of Cr leads to detrimental phase formation that compromises oxidation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 summarizes the trend of oxide weight gain on different component coating surfaces after 50 h continuous oxidation of laser cladding samples at 800 °C. It can be seen from Figure 6 that, after adding the Cr element based on WVTaTi (Cr0), the oxide weight gain decreases significantly. With the increase in oxidation time, the oxide weight-gain curve has continuity, and the content of Cr in the coating will affect the overall high-temperature oxidation resistance. In the first half of the experiment, the rate of oxidation weight increase is very fast, while, on the contrary, the rate of oxidation weight increase is slow after 20 h. Previous studies have shown that the high content of Cr in high-entropy alloys and the slow diffusion effect of high-entropy alloys can improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys [,,].

Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
